tagline: Diagrams, decision records and runbooks that turn a 3 a.m. page into a checklist.
overview: Documentation fails when it drifts. A diagram is drawn during a design review, the service gains three dependencies, and six months later the picture is a polite fiction. We rebuild the core set from what is actually running: the cloud APIs, the cluster, the pipeline definitions and the alert rules. Then we put it somewhere your team will maintain it, next to the code.

The runbooks matter most. Every alert that can wake someone up gets a page-long procedure: what the alert means, how to confirm it, the commands to run, and the point at which to stop and escalate. We test them during business hours by following them literally, because a runbook nobody has executed is a document, not a control.
problems: The architecture diagram is at least two years out of date
Alerts fire with no runbook and no clear owner
Onboarding a new engineer takes a full month
Design decisions get re-litigated because nobody recorded them

includes.title: Architecture diagrams
includes.text: Context, container and dependency diagrams generated from live infrastructure where possible, then reviewed with the engineers who own each service so errors get corrected early.

includes.title: Operational runbooks
includes.text: One runbook per alert, covering symptoms, confirmation steps, remediation commands, rollback and the escalation trigger, stored beside the code that produces the alert.

includes.title: Decision records
includes.text: Short architecture decision records capturing the options considered, the choice made and the consequences accepted, so a question from two years ago has an answer.

includes.title: Onboarding paths
includes.text: A first-week guide for each role: accounts to request, repositories to read, a small first task and the people to ask about each system.

includes.title: Documentation as code
includes.text: Everything lives in Markdown in your repositories, reviewed in pull requests and published by the same pipeline that ships the service it describes.

includes.title: Freshness checks
includes.text: Scheduled checks that flag runbooks untouched after a related service change and diagrams that no longer match the infrastructure they claim to show.

deliverables: Architecture diagram set for your main services
A runbook for every alert that pages
Architecture decision record template and backlog
Onboarding guide for each engineering role
Documentation repository wired into your pipeline

process.title: Inventory what exists
process.text: We collect the diagrams, wikis, runbooks and tribal knowledge that exist today, then compare them against the systems and alerts that are actually live.

process.title: Write the core set
process.text: Architecture diagrams, alert runbooks and decision records are drafted with your engineers, not for them, so the content is accurate and someone already owns it.

process.title: Test every runbook
process.text: We execute each procedure in a non-production environment, correct the steps that do not work, and add the rollback and escalation detail that was missing.

process.title: Wire in the cadence
process.text: Documentation lands in your repositories with a review checklist, a stale-content check and an owner named against every page so drift is visible.

faqs.q: Our engineers will not maintain documentation. Why would this be different?
faqs.a: Because it lives in the repositories they already work in, changes with the code in the same pull request, and is checked automatically when it goes stale. If a page needs a separate tool and a separate login, it will rot; ours does not.

faqs.q: Can you document a system that nobody fully understands?
faqs.a: That is a common starting point and part of the work. We read the code, the infrastructure and the logs, interview whoever has been closest to it, and mark our uncertainty explicitly rather than guessing. Gaps get listed as questions for the team to confirm.

faqs.q: Who owns the documentation when you leave?
faqs.a: Your team does, from day one. Everything sits in your repositories under your accounts, with named owners per area and a review cadence. We are not the only people who can edit it, and that is deliberate.

faqs.q: How do you keep diagrams from going stale?
faqs.a: Where a diagram can be generated from infrastructure, we generate it and review the output on a schedule. Where it cannot, the diagram is tied to a service owner and checked in the same review as the next change to that service.
